messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have two questions based on the message and 2 warnings I obtained:

1. Where do I set "smooth_check = TRUE"? I want to later run a multivariate GWAS using parallel processing.

2. Is the S matrix referred to in the message I get the LDSCoutput$S (the covariance matrix on the liability scale for case/control designs) or the LDSCoutput$V (the sampling covariance matrix in the format expected by lavaan)?

I added the LDSCoutput$S and LDSCoutput$V files as attachments.

Thank you for your patience. I am a beginner!

Camille

CommonFactor_DWLS<- commonfactor(covstruc = LDSCoutput, estimation="DWLS")
[1] "Running Model"
[1] "Calculating CFI" elapsed 0.593
 1] "The S matrix was smoothed prior to model estimation due to a non-positive definite matrix. The largest absolute difference in a cell between the smoothed and non-smoothed matrix was 0.0744047829376131 As a result of the smoothing, the largest Z-statistic change for the genetic covariances was 1.80833280592617 . We recommend setting the smooth_check argument to true if you are going to run a multivariate GWAS."

Warning messages:

1: In commonfactor(covstruc = LDSCoutput, estimation = "DWLS") : A difference greater than .025 was observed pre- and post-smoothing in the genetic covariance matrix. This reflects a large difference and results should be interpreted with caution!! This can often result from including low powered traits, and you might consider removing those traits from the model. If you are going to run a multivariate GWAS we strongly recommend setting the smooth_check argument to true to check smoothing for each SNP.

2: In commonfactor(covstruc = LDSCoutput, estimation = "DWLS") : A difference greater than .025 was observed pre- and post-smoothing for Z-statistics in the genetic covariance matrix. This reflects a large difference and results should be interpreted with caution!! This can often result from including low powered traits, and you might consider removing those traits from the model. If you are going to run a multivariate GWAS we strongly recommend setting the smooth_check argument to true to check smoothing for each SNP.

messages.subject: Re: smooth_check, LDSCoutput$S and LDSCoutput$V
messages.body_plain:
Hi Camille,

Good questions! Answers below:
1. I was actually behind on adding in the smooth_check argument so your post gave me the push to sit down and put that code in for the multivariate GWAS functions (userGWAS and commonfactorGWAS). Since I just updated that today you will want to reinstall Genomic SEM and restart R before running the multivariate GWAS, but you can now set smooth_check = TRUE within the context of either GWAS function. Since this functionality is new definitely let me know if you run into any issues or hard to make sense of error messages!

2. The S matrix refers to the genetic covariance matrix reflected in LDSCoutput$S. Smoothing of .07 at the level of the S matrix is fairly large and, as the warning you posted notes, you can certainly try and safeguard against false positives or negatives by setting smooth_check to TRUE and pruning out multivariate GWAS results that require a high degree of smoothing. However, you might also consider re-examining what traits you are choosing to include in the model as high levels of smoothing are typically a consequence of the more low powered traits. So if you have one particular trait among many that is low powered, you could try rerunning the model with that trait excluded and see how much smoothing still occurs.

Best,
  Andrew

messages.subject: Confusing results with genomic SEM - higher-order p factor models
messages.subject_clean: Confusing results with genomic SEM - higher-order p factor models
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone!

I have specified two models in genomic SEM: a p-factor and a higher
order p-factor model (both include the same internalizing and externalizing
traits). I obtained summary statistics for the p factors and for internalizing
and externalizing components with the userGWAS function, and I used these
sumstats to compute PRS for the p-factors.

Unfortunately, my p factor PRS have very low or negative
correlations with the PRS for the externalizing and internalizing traits (many correlations
are ~0.005). This does not make sense, as I used the same summary
statistics for the genomic SEM analyses and for calculating the trait PRS. These correlations also
contradict the genetic (LDSC) correlations I obtained between my p-factor summary statistics and the trait summary statistics.

If you would have any ideas on what might have gone wrong in the
process, or on checks I could do to better understand my results, I would
appreciate it so much!

A few more details on the analyses: to
avoid negative residual variances, I placed constraints on some of the trait
residuals. My model fit was decent for both the simple p factor and the higher
order model (CFI > 0.9, SRMR < .10), and the standardized
estimates made sense. I calculated the PRS in a genetic dataset that has no
sample overlap with the GWAS used for the genomic SEM analyses.

I am also attaching images for the model specification and fit, the genetic (LDSC) correlations and the correlations between the PRS, in
case this can be helpful.

Thank you for your attention!

Liliana

messages.subject: Re: GWAS by subtraction
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nicola,

Thanks for posting that output! I think one issue is that the effective sample size formula (at least the one we post on the Genomic SEM wiki) is breaking down when using unit variance identification for the factors. This is something we need to document better, but the default of our GWAS functions is to use unit loading ID, in which case the h^2 of the latent factor is scaled relative to the observed h^2 of the factor indicators, and effective sample size estimates can be interpreted in light of this scaling.

In the case of a GWAS-by-subtraction model, where you are forced to use unit variance identification as you have correctly specified in your model, you are specifying a model in which the h^2 of the factor is 100%, relative to the h^2 of the indicators being on the order < 7%. So assuming a highly heritable GWAS target (i.e., the latent factor) the effective sample size formula is essentially telling you that you must not have been very high powered to begin with (i.e., had a small effective sample size) given the estimates you get and the high heritability of the trait. All that to say, I would not use the effective sample size formula in this case as a metric of power. However, the ratio of beta/SE will be approximately the same regardless of what form of model identification you use. The lower heritability of your items may be compounding this issue, but to get a sense of power pre and post GWAS-by-subtraction I'd then suggest taking a look at metrics like mean chi-square, QQ-plots, etc. and if those still look highly attenuated then happy to talk further to help diagnose the issue.

Best,
  Andrew
